64.title: Two dreams in a cell
64.hook: two prisoners ask about their dreams, and Yusuf first speaks to them of the One
64.howItsDone: Muslims often cite Yusuf in prison as a model of da'wa, sharing faith with kindness and honesty; his address "my two companions of the prison" is quoted as an example of gentle speech.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: prison, chosen, and a man who asked for help not to slip. Your line was the prison was freer. Did you choose the harder right thing? Day sixty-four.
screen: `THE PRISON WAS FREER.`

segments.voice: A hospital ward, a barracks, a long night shift: in hard places, people find each other. They talk. They trade stories. They ask each other the questions they'd never ask at home. Two young men go into prison with Yusuf. The Qur'an says they'd noticed something about him: we see you're one of those who do good. And each of them comes to him with a dream. The first says: I saw myself pressing grapes for wine. The second says: I saw myself carrying bread on my head, and birds were eating from it. Tell us what it means. Today: two dreams in a cell.
screen: `PEOPLE FIND EACH OTHER.` → `YOU'RE ONE WHO DOES GOOD.` → `WINE, AND BREAD FOR BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. Yusuf has the answer. And he makes them wait, not to be clever, but because he has something he wants to give them first. He says: before your next meal arrives, I'll tell you. This is part of what my Lord has taught me. And then he tells them who he is: I follow the way of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub. There's Ibrahim again, the one who looked at the stars and loved what doesn't set, weeks ago on this path. Then Yusuf speaks to them tenderly. The Arabic is ya sahibayi s-sijn: my two companions of the prison. Not you criminals. Not you poor souls. Companions. And he asks them a question: many separate lords, or Allah, the One, the Overwhelming? The decision, he says, belongs to Allah alone. That's the heart of it for Yusuf. Before he tells them anything about their future, he tells them about the One. Then he answers, straight. One of you will pour wine for his master again. The other will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter you asked about is decided. It isn't a gentle answer, but it's honest. And then, a human moment. To the one he knew would be freed, Yusuf says: mention me to your master. And the verse says Satan made him forget, so Yusuf stayed in prison a few more years. The Qur'an's word for that stretch is bid', a handful. It doesn't give the number; commentators usually explain it as three to nine. Some good you do, the world forgets for years.
screen: `BEFORE YOUR NEXT MEAL.` · `MY TWO COMPANIONS OF THE PRISON.` · `THE ONE, BEFORE THE FUTURE.` · `MENTION ME — AND HE FORGOT.` · then, large: `START WITH THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share something kind before you're asked. Settle, and breathe. Yusuf gave his cellmates something before they got what they came for. Think of who's sharing a hard place with you right now: a coworker on the same long project, a family member in the same waiting room, a classmate in the same impossible course. What could you give them before they ask? A word of encouragement. A coffee. A sincere compliment. Calling them companion, in whatever way you say it. Pick one person and one thing. If you pray, you can ask to be good company. The bell holds the time.
Two dreams in a cell. Wine and bread, two cellmates, and a prophet who spoke of the One before he spoke of their futures. Today's word.
screen: `TWO DREAMS IN A CELL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: start with the one. Today, in a hard place, begin with what matters most before you get to what's urgent. Day sixty-four.

65.title: Seven fat cows
65.hook: the cupbearer finally remembers, and Yusuf reads the king's dream as seven good years and seven hard
65.carry: the fat years feed the thin
65.howItsDone: Muslims draw practical wisdom from Yusuf's interpretation, saving and planning in times of plenty, and often cite it in teaching about stewardship and preparing for hardship.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: two dreams in a cell, and a prophet who called his cellmates companions. Your line was start with the one. Did you begin with what matters most? Day sixty-five.
screen: `START WITH THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Years pass. Yusuf is still in prison, forgotten by the man who promised to mention him. And then the king of Egypt has a dream that won't leave him alone. He tells his court: I saw seven fat cows, and seven lean cows eating them. And seven green ears of grain, and seven others, dry. Tell me what it means. His advisers have no answer. Jumbled dreams, they say, and we don't know how to read those. And the freed prisoner, the one who pours the king's wine, hears it all. The Qur'an says he remembered, after a long time. Send me, he says. I know someone. Today: seven fat cows.
screen: `FORGOTTEN, FOR YEARS.` → `THE KING'S DREAM.` → `THE CUPBEARER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. The cupbearer comes to the cell and says: Yusuf, you truthful one, explain this dream to us. Notice: truthful one. Years later, he still remembers the thing that mattered about Yusuf. And now watch what Yusuf does. He doesn't say, first get me out of here. He doesn't say, you forgot me. He doesn't bargain at all. He answers, and goes further than he was asked. He says: for seven years, farm as you usually do. What you harvest, leave in the ear, on the stalk, except the little you eat. Then seven hard years will come that eat up what you stored, except a little you keep back. Then a year will come when people have rain, and they'll press fruit and oil again. The king asked for a meaning. Yusuf gives him a plan. Save in the good years. Store the grain in the ear, where it keeps. Eat a little, not a lot. And then he adds a year the dream never mentioned, a fifteenth year of relief. That's what a hopeful reader of dreams does: he sees past the famine to the rain. Jews and Christians tell this story too, in Genesis, where Joseph reads Pharaoh's dream in much the same way. And the lesson carries straight into an ordinary life. Good seasons don't last. Hard seasons don't either. The wise thing is to let the fat years feed the thin. And Yusuf, still in his cell, has just given Egypt a way through the hard years without asking for a thing.
screen: `YUSUF, YOU TRUTHFUL ONE.` · `NO BARGAIN, JUST THE ANSWER.` · `LEAVE IT IN THE EAR.` · `A YEAR OF RAIN AFTER.` · then, large: `THE FAT YEARS FEED THE THIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: save one thing today for later. Settle, and breathe. Think about what you have plenty of right now. It might be money this week, or energy, or time, or patience, or a friend's goodwill. Whatever season you're in, there's usually something that's fat right now. Choose one small portion to put by. Five dollars into savings. A meal into the freezer. An hour of rest before the busy week. A kind message to someone before you need them. Picture putting it away, in the ear. If you pray, you can give thanks for the plenty. The bell holds the time.
Seven fat cows. The king's dream, and Yusuf's plan: save in the seven good years to live through the seven hard. Today's word.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the fat years feed the thin. Put one small thing away today for a harder week you can't see yet. Day sixty-five.

66.title: "I do not absolve myself"
66.hook: cleared of all charges, Yusuf still says the self urges toward wrong unless Allah has mercy
66.howItsDone: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs, the self, as a lifelong part of faith; Muslim teachers, Sufis especially, use the Qur'an's three descriptions (the self that urges wrong, the self that blames itself, the self at peace) to describe that journey.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven fat cows, and a plan for the hard years. Your line was the fat years feed the thin. Did you put one thing away? Day sixty-six.
screen: `THE FAT YEARS FEED THE THIN.`

segments.voice: Years in a cell, for something he didn't do. Then a messenger is at the door: the king wants you. A man in that cell could be out the door before the sentence was finished. The king has heard Yusuf's reading of the dream and says: bring him to me. And Yusuf, still in the cell, says to the messenger: no. Go back to your master, and ask him about the women who cut their hands. He won't walk out under a cloud. He wants the truth said out loud first. Today's word is what he says about himself once it is.
screen: `THE DOOR OPENS.` → `NOT YET.` → `ASK ABOUT THE WOMEN.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf. The king calls in the women. They say: Allah preserve us, we know no evil of him. And the Aziz's wife stands up and says it herself: now the truth is out. I tried to turn him from himself, and he is one of the truthful. Total vindication. And then comes a line commentators have argued over. In Pickthall's translation: "I do not exculpate myself." I don't clear myself. The self, the nafs, urges toward wrong, except the one my Lord has mercy on. Who says it? Commentators such as al-Tabari say Yusuf: at the very moment he's declared innocent, he refuses to call himself pure. Other scholars, including Ibn Kathir, read it as the Aziz's wife, still speaking, owning her part. The Arabic allows both. Our path follows the first reading, and it's worth knowing the second is there. Either way, look at the word. Nafs. It means the self, the soul, and it shares a root with nafas, breath. And the Qur'an describes it at different stages. Here it's the nafs that urges toward wrong. Elsewhere it's the self that blames itself when it slips. And near the end of the Qur'an, it's the self at peace, called back to its Lord, well-pleased. Muslim teachers, especially in the Sufi tradition, have seen a whole journey there: from the self that pushes, to the self that notices, to the self that rests. What Yusuf gives us is the first honest step. Even innocent, even vindicated, he doesn't say, I'm fine. He says: I'm a self, and selves need mercy. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once said that if he'd been kept in prison as long as Yusuf, he'd have answered the summons at once. He was honoring Yusuf's patience.
screen: `THE TRUTH IS OUT.` · `I DO NOT CLEAR MYSELF.` · `YUSUF, OR THE AZIZ'S WIFE?` · `THE SELF THAT PUSHES, THEN RESTS.` · then, large: `NAFS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch your own self honestly for a minute. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to fix anything. Just watch your mind like you'd watch a busy street from a window. Notice what it reaches for. A craving. A grudge. A little self-congratulation. A worry. Notice how often it wants to be right, to be seen, to be comfortable. No scolding. Just seeing. Then, near the end, say inside, the way Yusuf did: I don't clear myself. If you pray, you can ask for mercy on the self you just watched. The bell holds the time.
Nafs. The self, the soul: the part of you that pushes, that can learn to notice, and can come to rest. Today's word.
screen: `NAFS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I don't clear myself. When you win an argument today, or get proven right, pause, and don't let it go to your head. Day sixty-six.

67.title: The brothers at the gate
67.hook: famine brings the brothers to Egypt, they don't recognize him, and he keeps his youngest brother with the cup in his bag
67.howItsDone: Muslims read Yusuf's generosity to his brothers as a model of restraint and kindness toward those who have done wrong, and Ya'qub's words, Allah is the best guardian, are often repeated when entrusting loved ones to Allah.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: nafs, the self that pushes, notices, and can rest. Your line was I don't clear myself. Did you catch the self wanting to be right? Day sixty-seven.
screen: `I DON'T CLEAR MYSELF.`

segments.voice: A face from years ago, someone who once did real harm, standing a few feet away. One person knows everything. The other sees a stranger. Yusuf is out of prison now. He asked the king to put him in charge of the storehouses, and the good years have come and gone. Now the hard years are here, just as he said. The hard years reach an old man and his sons in the land where Yusuf grew up. And one day, in the line of hungry travelers waiting for grain, Yusuf looks up and sees faces he'd know anywhere, his brothers. Today: the brothers at the gate.
screen: `OUT OF PRISON, OVER THE STORES.` → `THE FAMINE REACHES HOME.` → `FACES HE KNOWS IN THE LINE.`

segments.voice: Surah Yusuf, verse fifty-eight: they came in to him, and he knew them, and they did not know him. In Arabic, fa-'arafahum wa-hum lahu munkirun. The whole story in a line. The last time they saw him, he was a boy going down a well. Now he's the man who decides whether their family eats. He gives them their grain, generously. He even has their payment slipped back into their saddlebags. But he asks for one thing: next time, bring your youngest brother, your father's other son. Without him, don't come back. At home, Ya'qub doesn't want to let the youngest go. He's lost one son already on a trip with these brothers. In the end he makes them swear to bring him back and says: Allah is the best guardian. They return with the youngest, and Yusuf takes him aside and tells him quietly: I am your brother. Don't grieve over what they did. Then he has the king's drinking cup placed in that brother's bag. A herald shouts: you're thieves! The cup is found. And the brothers, under pressure, say something ugly: if he stole, well, a brother of his stole before. They mean Yusuf, to his face, without knowing it. And the Qur'an says Yusuf kept it in his heart and did not reveal it to them. He just thought: you're in a worse place than that. Why keep his brother? Commentators say it was a way, permitted to him, to keep the youngest safe with him. Some readers also see a test in it: would the brothers abandon another of their father's sons, the way they once did? Tomorrow the story answers.
screen: `HE KNEW THEM; THEY DIDN'T.` · `BRING YOUR YOUNGEST BROTHER.` · `I AM YOUR BROTHER.` · `THE CUP IN THE BAG.` · then, large: `HE KEPT IT IN HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be generous to someone who hurt you. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who once wronged you, not the deepest wound, something you can hold. Picture them in front of you, not knowing everything you know. Now picture giving them something anyway. Their full portion. A fair word. A favor they don't expect. Not because what they did was fine. Because you'd like to be the kind of person who fills the sacks. Notice what that does in your chest. If you pray, you can ask for good for them. The bell holds the time.
The brothers at the gate. Hungry travelers, and the brother they threw away, who knew them when they didn't know him. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: he knew them. If someone who hurt you crosses your path today, give them their full portion, and keep the rest in your heart. Day sixty-seven.

68.title: "No blame on you today"
68.hook: a grieving father who never despairs, a brother who forgives, and a shirt that brings back sight
68.tomorrow: the vow and the fruit out of season
68.howItsDone: Muslims often recall Yusuf's words to his brothers when making peace after a quarrel, and many read Surah Yusuf in full as a story of patience, trust and forgiveness.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers at the gate: hungry, asking for grain, with no idea who was filling their sacks. Your line was he knew them. Did you manage one kindness toward someone who once hurt you? Day sixty-eight, the last day of Yusuf.
screen: `HE KNEW THEM.`

segments.voice: The brothers go home without the youngest, and the eldest stays behind in Egypt, unwilling to face his father. First Yusuf, years ago, and now his little brother too. Ya'qub turns away from them, and the Qur'an says his eyes went white with grief. His sons think he'll grieve himself to death. And he answers: “I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah.” Then, of all things, he sends them back. Go, he says, look for Yusuf and his brother, and “despair not of the Spirit of Allah.” So they return to Egypt a third time, poor, embarrassed, begging for a little grain as charity. And the powerful man across the table asks them a quiet question. Do you know what you did to Yusuf? They stare at him. Wait. Are you Yusuf?
screen: `A FATHER'S EYES GO WHITE.` → `DESPAIR NOT.` → `ARE YOU YUSUF?`

segments.voice: I am Yusuf, he says, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us. They threw him in a well. They sold him for a few coins. They lied to their father with a shirt and false blood. He spent years as a servant and years in a prison. He holds the grain of Egypt, and they're standing in front of him with empty sacks. The brothers admit it: Allah has preferred you over us, and we were wrong. And Yusuf's answer, in Arabic, is la tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm. No blame on you today. No reproach, no scolding, no list of what you did. And then, may Allah forgive you, and He is the most merciful of those who show mercy. He doesn't make them earn it. He doesn't wait for them to grovel. Then the shirt comes back into the story, one last time. The first shirt came home with false blood on it. The second was torn from behind and proved him innocent. Now Yusuf sends a third: lay this on my father's face. Before the caravan even arrives, Ya'qub says, I can smell Yusuf. The shirt touches his face, and he sees again. Finally the whole family comes to Egypt. Yusuf raises his parents up beside him, and they all bow down. And Yusuf says: “This is the interpretation of my dream of old.” Eleven stars, the sun and the moon, from the very first day of this story. Notice one more thing. When Yusuf tells the story back, he says Shaytan made trouble between me and my brothers. Even then, he won't name them as the villains. Muslims remember that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, years later, is reported to have answered his own old enemies in Mecca with these same words of Yusuf.
screen: `I AM YUSUF, AND THIS IS MY BROTHER.` · `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.` · `THE THIRD SHIRT: HIS FATHER SEES.` · `THE DREAM COMES TRUE.` · then, large: `DESPAIR NOT OF THE SPIRIT OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one old thing, out loud. Settle, and breathe. Let one old hurt come up, not the biggest one, just one that still stings a little. A friend who didn't show up. A sibling who said the wrong thing years ago. Picture their face. Then say it, quietly, out loud, just to the room: no blame on you today. You don't have to feel it all the way. Today is enough. If you pray, you can ask Allah to forgive them, the way Yusuf did. The bell holds the time.
No blame on you today. La tathriba 'alaykumu l-yawm: Yusuf's words to the brothers who threw him in a well. No reproach, only forgiveness.

69.title: The vow and the fruit out of season
69.word: The vow and the fruit out of sea
69.hook: a mother gives her unborn child to Allah, and an old guardian finds fruit that shouldn't be there
69.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Maryam's birth in Surah Al 'Imran and honor her as one of the best of women; some use her answer, 'it is from Allah', as a way of receiving unexpected good.

screen: `DAY SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Yusuf, and his words to the brothers who sold him: no blame on you today. Did you let one old thing go? Today, a new story. Day sixty-nine.
screen: `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.`

segments.voice: A woman is expecting a child, and she makes a promise before the baby is even born. She tells Allah: whatever is in my womb, I give it to You, set apart for Your service. In her world, that meant a son, a boy raised to serve in the house of worship. And then the baby comes, and it's a girl. You can almost hear her surprise in the Qur'an. My Lord, I've given birth to a girl, she says, and the Qur'an adds that Allah knew best what she had delivered. She keeps the vow anyway. She names her daughter Maryam, and asks Allah to protect her and her children from Shaytan. This is how the Qur'an begins the story of Maryam: with her mother.
screen: `A PROMISE BEFORE THE BIRTH.` → `IT'S A GIRL.` → `HER NAME IS MARYAM.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an calls her mother simply the wife of 'Imran. It doesn't give her a name; later tradition calls her Hannah. And the whole family gives its name to a surah: Al 'Imran, the family of 'Imran, the third chapter. Here's what happens next. Allah accepts the girl with a beautiful acceptance, the verse says, and makes her grow up well. And an old man named Zakariyya becomes her guardian. Maryam lives and prays in a small room in the place of worship, a mihrab. The same word now names the niche in a mosque's wall that shows which way to pray. And every time Zakariyya goes in to see her, he finds food there. Food he didn't bring. So he asks her, in Pickthall's old English: “O Mary! Whence cometh unto thee this (food)?” Where does this come from? And the girl answers, simply: “It is from Allah. Allah giveth without stint to whom He will.” Without stint. In Arabic, bi-ghayri hisab: without counting, without reckoning, not measured out on a scale. Early commentators said Zakariyya found summer fruit in winter, and winter fruit in summer. The verse itself only says food, so that detail is theirs, not the text's. Now notice who teaches whom. The old guardian, the man of prayer, asks the question. The girl gives the answer. And one more thing worth knowing: commentators point out that Maryam is the only woman the Qur'an calls by her own name. A whole surah, the nineteenth, is named for her. Muslims honor her as one of the best women who ever lived.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a gift that came from nowhere. Sit, and breathe. Go back over the last week and look for something you didn't plan and didn't earn. A text from an old friend. A parking spot. A stranger's kindness. A song at the right moment. Something that was simply there when you walked in, like fruit in Maryam's room. Hold it for a moment. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. If not, just let yourself be surprised by it again. The bell holds the time.
The vow and the fruit out of season. A mother gives her child to Allah, and the child is fed with food no one brought. Bi-ghayri hisab: without measure.
screen: `THE VOW AND THE FRUIT OUT OF SEASON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: from allah, without measure. Today, when something good arrives that you didn't plan, stop and ask Maryam's question: where did this come from? Tomorrow, the old guardian prays. Day sixty-nine.

70.title: Zakariyya's quiet prayer
70.hook: an old man with gray hair and no children prays in a whisper, and is given a son named Yahya
70.tomorrow: the messenger in the eastern place
70.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a aloud and in private; Zakariyya's prayer for a child, in Surah Maryam, Surah Al 'Imran and Surah Al-Anbiya (21:89), is one that couples hoping for a child sometimes recite.

screen: `DAY SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, fruit in Maryam's room that nobody brought. Your line was from Allah without measure. What turned up unplanned? Day seventy, the end of week ten.
screen: `FROM ALLAH, WITHOUT MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Stay in that little room for a minute longer. Zakariyya has just heard the girl in his care say that the food came from Allah, who gives without counting. And something stirs in him. He's old. His bones are weak, his hair has gone white, and his wife has never been able to have children. For years that door has been closed, and he's stopped knocking. Food nobody brought, in a room nobody entered. And right there, the Qur'an says, he prayed. Not loudly. Not in front of anyone. The nineteenth surah, the one named for Maryam, opens with exactly this: an old man, alone, whispering.
screen: `AN OLD MAN IN THE ROOM OF PRAYER.` → `A DOOR CLOSED FOR YEARS.` → `RIGHT THERE, HE PRAYED.`

segments.voice: Pickthall's translation of Surah Maryam puts it like this: “When he cried unto his Lord a cry in secret.” In Arabic, nida'an khafiyya. A call, a hidden one. Why secret? Commentators offered a few reasons. A quiet prayer is closer to sincerity: no one to impress. Or maybe he felt a little shy, asking for a baby at his age. And listen to how he makes his case. My bones are weak, he says, and my head is shining with gray hair. Then the line that holds the whole prayer together: “I have never been unblest in prayer to Thee, my Lord.” In other words: every time I've asked, You've been good to me. That's his reason for hoping. Not his strength, not his record. Just a lifetime of being answered. He asks for an heir, someone to carry on the family of Ya'qub, someone pleasing to Allah. And the answer comes, through angels, while he's standing in prayer: good news of a son, and his name is Yahya. The Qur'an says no one had been given that name before. Zakariyya is astonished. How, when I'm this old and my wife is barren? And he's told: it is easy for your Lord. Then he asks for a sign, and the sign is silence: for three nights he won't be able to speak to people, though he's well. The man who prayed in a whisper is given days of quiet. Christians know this child too, as John the Baptist. And that closes week ten: two dreams in a cell, seven fat cows, a heart that doesn't clear itself, brothers at the gate, no blame on you today, fruit without measure, and a whisper that was heard.
screen: `A CRY IN SECRET.` · `MY HEAD IS SHINING WITH GRAY HAIR.` · `NEVER UNBLEST IN PRAYER TO THEE.` · `A SON NAMED YAHYA, AND A SILENCE.` · then, large: `HE CALLED IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one thing you've quietly given up on. A hope you stopped mentioning. A person you stopped expecting to change. A door you stopped knocking on. Don't argue with it. Just name it, inside. If you pray, you can ask for it again, quietly, the way Zakariyya did, with no one listening. If you don't, just let yourself hope for it for two minutes, without defending the hope. The bell holds the time.
Zakariyya's quiet prayer. An old man's hidden call, nida'an khafiyya, whispered where no one could hear, and answered with a son called Yahya.
